title: Marketing Agency Fees: The Real Cost Beyond the Retainer
summary: Calculate marketing agency fees beyond the retainer, including internal time, delays, and hidden costs. Use this model before you hire.
body_markdown:
Marketing agency fees include far more than the monthly retainer. Your actual cost combines the agency invoice, internal briefing and approval time, separate creative work, onboarding charges, and revenue lost when campaigns wait in a queue.


If you spend $10,000 to $100,000 per month on paid media, the agency retainer is easy to see. The harder costs show up in calendar blocks, Slack threads, missed test windows, and repeated explanations after an account manager changes.

## What marketing agency fees look like in 2026


Most paid media agencies use one of three pricing models: a percentage of ad spend, a flat monthly retainer, or a hybrid of both.


As of October 1, 2026, ecommerce and startup brands commonly see paid media retainers between $2,000 and $10,000 per month. Percentage-of-spend pricing often falls between 10% and 20% of managed ad spend. A hybrid agreement usually pairs a lower base retainer with a spend percentage, performance fee, or separate creative charge.


The pricing model matters less than the operating model behind it. A $4,000 retainer becomes expensive if your team spends 20 hours each month preparing briefs, correcting reporting, approving routine changes, and reconstructing account history. A $10,000 retainer can be a good deal if the agency ships profitable creative quickly and gives your team clear decisions to make.


Agencies also bill for work that founders often assume comes with media management:


- One-time setup or onboarding fees
- Creative strategy, production, editing, and creator sourcing
- Landing page design or conversion-rate optimization
- Analytics implementation and attribution work
- Feed management for Google Shopping and Meta catalogs
- Quarterly business reviews and custom reporting


Ask for the full scope before you compare proposals. A lower retainer often excludes the work that actually improves performance.


## The real cost of hiring an agency


The cost of hiring an agency equals the invoice plus the work your company must do to make that agency effective. It also includes the cost of waiting for decisions or campaign changes.


Paid media is not a set-and-forget channel. Meta, Google Ads, TikTok, and Amazon campaigns need fresh creative, budget changes, audience exclusions, landing page feedback, and rapid responses to inventory or margin shifts. Every handoff adds delay.


A typical operating cycle looks like this:


1. Your team identifies a problem or opportunity.
2. Someone writes a brief or sends context in Slack.
3. The agency account manager converts that request into a task.
4. A media buyer or creative team reviews it.
5. Your team approves the proposed change.
6. The agency makes the update.
7. Reporting explains the result in the next meeting.


That sequence works for large strategic changes. It is slow for routine testing.


The hidden labor usually falls on the people whose time is most expensive. Founders review creative because brand risk sits with them. Marketing leads fill knowledge gaps because the agency lacks product context. Designers rework assets because the original brief did not include platform requirements. Finance teams answer questions about margin, promotions, and inventory.


Account manager turnover compounds the problem. A new contact needs to learn your best sellers, attribution rules, creative approvals, discount calendar, customer segments, and past tests. Your agency may document this well. Your team still spends time rebuilding context.


Reporting creates another cost when it describes activity rather than drives a decision. “CPA increased 12% week over week” is an observation. “Pause two prospecting ad sets, move $3,000 to the winning product bundle, and test a new first-frame hook” gives your team a decision.


## A cost model for agency retainers


The following model uses a fully loaded internal rate of $75 per hour. It is not a market benchmark. It shows why the visible agency retainer rarely represents your total monthly cost.


Monthly ad spend Agency retainer Internal hours per month Internal time cost Effective monthly cost Typical iteration speed


$10,000 $2,000 12 $900 $2,900 3 to 5 business days


$50,000 $6,000 20 $1,500 $7,500 2 to 4 business days


$100,000 $12,000 30 $2,250 $14,250 1 to 3 business days


The iteration-speed column deserves as much scrutiny as the cost column. If an ad has a weak hook, a broken product feed, or a budget cap, three business days is a long time to wait. That delay affects learning velocity, not only labor cost.


Your internal hourly rate should include salary, benefits, payroll taxes, management overhead, and the value of time diverted from higher-priority work. A founder spending four hours each month on agency approvals does not cost the same as a junior coordinator spending four hours.


Creative volume changes the equation fast. A brand running Meta prospecting successfully may need several fresh concepts each month. If the agency charges separately for each asset, include that cost in the model rather than treating it as an occasional add-on.


## How to calculate your hidden agency cost


Start with the last 30 days, not an ideal future process. Pull calendars, Slack threads, project tickets, agency emails, and approval requests. Count the time people actually spent supporting paid media.


Cost category How to calculate it Example monthly amount


Agency management fee Retainer plus percentage-of-spend charges $6,000


Founder or executive time Hours spent × loaded hourly rate 4 hours × $125 = $500


Marketing lead time Briefs, reviews, meetings, follow-up, and reporting 8 hours × $85 = $680


Creative and design support Internal production hours × loaded hourly rate 10 hours × $65 = $650


Finance and operations support Margin, inventory, promotion, and invoice work 2 hours × $60 = $120


Separate agency services Creative, reporting, landing pages, or feed work $1,500


Total operating cost Add every monthly line item $9,450


Then measure delay. Review five recent requests, such as pausing an ad, launching a promotion, changing spend, uploading creative, or correcting a catalog issue. Record the time between request and completion.


A median turnaround time tells you more than a service-level agreement buried in a contract. If urgent requests move quickly but normal tests wait six days, your experimentation system is slower than it appears.


Include onboarding fees in your first-quarter budget. An agency charging $5,000 for setup adds $1,667 per month to the first 90 days of a $5,000 monthly retainer. That does not make the fee unreasonable. It means you should judge early performance against the real investment.


## In-house vs agency cost: where each model wins


The in-house vs agency cost decision is not a simple salary-versus-retainer comparison. It is a choice between outside specialization and internal context.


Agencies win when you need a capable paid media function quickly. They bring category experience, channel-specific media buyers, creative production capacity, and established working knowledge of ad platforms. Some agencies also have useful relationships with Meta, Google, TikTok, or Amazon representatives. A strong agency is especially valuable when you have no internal buyer, no testing process, and no time to build one.


An in-house hire wins when paid media has become a daily operating function. A dedicated operator learns your margins, product roadmap, merchandising calendar, stock constraints, and customer objections without a briefing cycle. They can change campaigns while information is fresh.


A blended model often fits brands spending $50,000 to $100,000 per month. Keep strategic ownership, creative direction, and performance accountability inside the company. Use specialists for channel launches, creative production spikes, attribution work, or periods when spend grows faster than your hiring plan.


Do not hire in-house solely to remove agency fees. A paid media manager without enough creative supply, analytics support, or decision authority will underperform. Do not retain an agency solely because replacing it feels risky. If your team supplies the strategy, creative, analysis, and daily decisions, the agency may have become an expensive execution queue.


## How to reduce paid media operating drag


Start by separating high-risk decisions from routine changes. Brand-sensitive creative, large budget shifts, and new channel tests deserve review. Pausing an obvious loser or reallocating a pre-approved daily budget should not require a meeting.


Write operating guardrails before you renegotiate a retainer or add headcount. Good guardrails specify:


- Maximum daily budget changes without approval
- Target CPA, MER, or contribution-margin thresholds
- Creative claims that require legal or brand review
- Inventory rules for products approaching stockouts
- Who owns final decisions for promotions and discounting
- Expected turnaround times for campaign edits and creative tests

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What percentage do agencies charge for paid media management?


Many agencies charge 10% to 20% of monthly ad spend for paid media management. Others charge a flat agency retainer, often between $2,000 and $10,000 per month for SMB and mid-market ecommerce work. Review minimum fees, creative costs, and onboarding charges before comparing offers.


### How do I calculate the cost of hiring an agency?


Add the agency retainer, percentage-of-spend fees, creative charges, onboarding costs, and internal labor. Calculate internal labor by multiplying each person’s monthly support hours by their fully loaded hourly cost. Include time spent in meetings, briefs, approvals, reporting reviews, and operational follow-up.


### When does hiring in-house cost less than an agency?


In-house usually becomes attractive when paid media needs daily attention and your company has enough creative, analytics, and management support around the buyer. The comparison should include benefits, recruiting, software, and management time. A lower salary does not create a lower operating cost if the hire lacks the resources to execute.


### Are agency retainers worth it for ecommerce brands?


An agency retainer is worth it when the agency brings skills or capacity your company does not have and turns changes around quickly. It becomes poor value when your internal team supplies most of the strategy, creative direction, and decisions. Measure turnaround time and internal support hours alongside ROAS or CPA.
